meta.title: Advanced setup: TLS, services, backups and SSO
meta.description: Run ai-memory seriously: deployment topologies, TLS through Caddy, nginx or Cloudflare Tunnel, system services, backups, routing, OIDC and measured limits.

hero.title: Advanced setup and infrastructure
hero.lede: For when the server leaves your laptop. Each topic is a diagram or a table, the shortest correct config, and a link to the full document on GitHub.

topologies.title: Four places it can run
topologies.lede: The binary is the same in all four. What changes is the bind address, and with it how much auth and encryption you owe.

figure.alt: Four deployment topologies side by side: laptop only with the server inside the laptop, a homelab box that two laptops connect to, a LAN server with a TLS shield in front of it, and a server reached through an outbound tunnel to a cloud edge.
figure.caption: Moving right adds reach, and every step to the right adds a requirement. There is no replication between servers in any of them: many machines reach one server.

items.name: Laptop only
items.runs: systemd user unit, launchd agent, or a container

items.name: Homelab box
items.auth: Bearer token and host allowlist, both required
items.runs: Docker with a healthcheck, or the AUR system service

items.name: LAN with TLS
items.auth: Root token, plus a user and an API key per person
items.tls: Yes. Caddy with its internal CA works without a domain
items.runs: Docker Compose with a Caddy sidecar

items.name: Tunnel
items.runs: Docker Compose with a cloudflared sidecar

topologies.stdio: A laptop can skip HTTP entirely with ai-memory serve --transport stdio. For a homelab, the repository ships a bin/deploy script with compose and env templates. Follow the homelab deploy walkthrough.

internet.title: Not for the open internet
internet.text: ai-memory is a single-tenant workstation and homelab service. It is not designed for direct exposure to the untrusted internet, and denial of service from hostile traffic is out of scope. Put a tunnel or a proxy with its own access control in front.

tls.title: TLS through a reverse proxy
tls.lede: ai-memory does not terminate TLS itself, by design. A bearer token authenticates a request. It does not encrypt it.

skip.title: You can skip TLS when
items: the agent talks to it over stdio
the server is loopback-only, for one user, and nobody opens /web from another machine
it is local development or a one-off experiment

need.title: You need TLS when
items: accounts exist, because aim_ keys then cross the network
the server is bound beyond loopback
you open /web from a different machine
the server is reachable beyond the LAN

figure.alt: Two laptops connect over HTTPS to a reverse proxy. The proxy forwards plain HTTP to ai-memory. The proxy and ai-memory sit on the same host.
figure.caption: The proxy owns the certificate. ai-memory stays on plain HTTP behind it, reachable only over the Docker network or loopback.

tls.caddy: For a public domain with ports 80 and 443 reachable. Caddy issues and renews the Let’s Encrypt certificate on its own. The repository has the full compose file as docker/compose.tls.caddy.yml.

caddyLan.text: No domain and nothing exposed. Caddy’s internal CA signs the certificate, and you install its root certificate once on every client machine. Skip that step and clients either refuse the connection or learn to click through warnings.
caddyLan.comment: tells Caddy to use the internal CA instead of LE

tls.nginx: For when you already run nginx and have certificate files. HTTP/1.1 and the empty Connection header are required for MCP’s streamable HTTP transport.

cloudflared.text: An outbound-only tunnel, so no ports open on your router. It needs a domain on Cloudflare, and the free tier works. In the dashboard, point the public hostname at http://ai-memory:49374. The full compose file is docker/compose.tls.cloudflared.yml.

server.title: Then tell the server
server.text: The allowlist must include the public hostname, or the DNS rebinding guard rejects the proxy’s requests. The secure cookie setting is required once people log in through a listener beyond loopback.

clients.title: And repoint the clients
clients.text: The MCP URL ends in /mcp. The hook URL is the bare origin.

tls.guide: Read the full HTTPS guide, including subpaths and proxy timeouts for long bootstrap runs

services.title: Keep the server running
services.lede: ai-memory does not restart itself. The service manager on each operating system does that.

user.text: For a single-user workstation. The AUR packages install the unit. It needs no sudo and keeps state in ~/.local/share/ai-memory. A user unit stops at logout unless you enable lingering.
user.lingerComment: keep it running after you log out

services.system: For a shared workstation or a LAN box. Data lives in /var/lib/ai-memory, config in /etc/ai-memory/config.toml, secrets in /etc/ai-memory/env. Do not run both units on the same bind address.
services.launchd: The macOS tarballs include a LaunchAgent plist with two placeholders. Run this from the extracted tarball. A LaunchAgent stops at logout, and macOS has no equivalent of lingering. Nothing rotates its two log files.
services.winsw: ai-memory has no Windows Service dispatcher, so sc create pointed at the exe does not work, and a Scheduled Task with Start-Process dies at the next reboot. WinSW wraps it. Use absolute paths: a service runs as LocalSystem, and %LOCALAPPDATA% would expand to the wrong profile.

links.systemd: systemd units in the install guide

data.title: The data directory and backups
data.lede: The wiki is the truth. It is plain markdown in a git repository, and the search index is built from it.

figure.alt: The data directory split in two. On the source of truth side: wiki, a git-versioned stack of markdown pages, and raw. On the derived side: db, models and logs. An arrow labelled reindex goes from wiki to db.
figure.caption: Reindex rebuilds pages, links and full-text search from the wiki. It does not bring back sessions, observations, handoffs, users, keys, audit rows or embeddings, so the database still belongs in your backup.

wiki.holds: Every page as markdown, in one git repository
wiki.backup: Yes. It is in the backup tarball, and you can also rsync it or git push it

raw.holds: Immutable, sanitized transcript segments from managed launches
raw.backup: Yes, if you use ai-memory run. Copy it separately

db.holds: memory.sqlite: full-text index, entities, embeddings, sessions, users, audit rows
db.backup: Yes. Pages, links and search rebuild from the wiki. Sessions, handoffs, users and keys live only here

models.holds: The local embedding model, about 87 MB
models.backup: No. It downloads again, or you place the files yourself

data.defaults: Defaults: ~/.local/share/ai-memory on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/ai-memory on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\ai-memory on Windows, /data in the container. Override with AI_MEMORY_DATA_DIR.

figure.alt: Backup takes a tar.gz archive from a running server. Restore goes from the archive into a stopped server, which is then started again.
figure.caption: Backup runs against a live server. Restore works directly on disk and refuses while any ai-memory process is alive.

save.title: Back up
save.text: It uses SQLite’s online backup API, so writes during the snapshot stay coherent. The tarball holds the wiki tree, the database snapshot and config.toml.

restore.title: Restore
restore.text: --data-dir is the host-side path of the volume. The paths here are the ones from the deploy guide. Use yours.
restore.restoreComment: Restore (sysinfo refuses if the container is still running).

oneServer.title: One server per data directory
oneServer.text: Two servers on one directory (a synced folder, an NFS mount, two containers on one volume) each run their own writer and git handle. SQLite survives it and the wiki does not. Since 2.0, serve takes an exclusive lock on .serve.lock, and a second server refuses to start and names the process holding it. The OS releases the lock when the process exits.

reindex.title: Rebuilding the index
reindex.text: ai-memory reindex --data-dir <path> needs the server stopped and a clean database. Take a backup, move db/memory.sqlite and its WAL and SHM files aside, run it, then run ai-memory embed after the restart to rebuild embeddings.

data.lifecycle: Read lifecycle operations: purge, rename, move, restore a page, reset

routing.title: Routing and identity
routing.lede: A shared server has to answer two questions: which project does this session belong to, and who is asking.

marker.title: The marker file
marker.text: By default the project is the name of the current directory, in a workspace called default. Drop a .ai-memory.toml in any ancestor directory to change that. Hooks walk up from the working directory and use the first marker they find.

items.title: Work and personal
items.text: One marker per parent directory. Every repository below it lands in that workspace, with the directory name as the project.

items.title: Mono-repo
items.text: A marker with a project pins every subdirectory to that one project. The closest marker wins.

items.title: Git worktrees
items.text: Linked worktrees and subdirectories resolve to the main repository, even when the worktree lives outside it.

marker.capture: The same file holds [capture] rules with ignore_paths, and ai-memory install-hooks --apply --capture-mode allowlist turns the marker into an opt-in: a repository without one emits no events. Native hooks enforce both. The Docker wrapper’s shell hooks do not. Read the marker file reference.

autoScope.title: Auto-scope modes
autoScope.text: An MCP call without an explicit project resolves through a “current project” pointer. The mode decides who shares that pointer. The server logs the live mode at startup.

modes.per_actor: The default. Isolates parallel harnesses and separate people on one server.
modes.per_session: For session-aware clients that forward the hook session id on every MCP request.
modes.single: The behaviour before v1.39. One slot for the whole process, last write wins. Unsafe on a shared server.

comments.max: hard cap; oldest insertions evicted first

sso.title: SSO and OIDC
sso.text: Each developer logs in once with an OIDC device flow against any standards-compliant issuer, such as Keycloak, Okta or Entra ID. The token then authenticates native lifecycle hooks and CLI commands when no static bearer token is set.
sso.calloutTitle: The server does not validate OIDC tokens
sso.calloutText: This is not a login gate for the server. ai-memory does not check OIDC tokens against your identity provider for API access. To put the server behind your IdP you need an OIDC-aware gateway or reverse proxy in front that translates accepted identities into a static bearer or a per-user API key. OIDC hook auth also needs the native hook path. The Docker wrapper’s shell hooks do not use it.
sso.link: Read the SSO and enterprise identity page

ops.title: Offline, limits and upgrades
ops.lede: What a security review, a capacity plan and a maintenance window each need to know.

airgapped.title: Air-gapped install

binaries.title: Binaries
binaries.text: Every release asset has a .sha256 file. Download on a connected machine, verify, carry it in. Releases carry checksums only, with no SLSA provenance or artifact attestation.

source.title: Source builds
source.text: SQLite is bundled and libgit2 is vendored, so the build needs a C toolchain and your crates mirror. cargo vendor works.

model.title: The embedding model
model.text: A default install fetches the model from Hugging Face on first start. For no outbound request at all, place model.safetensors, tokenizer.json and config.json in <data_dir>/models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/ beforehand. Checksums are pinned in source.

airgapped.telemetry: The binary has no telemetry. The Docker wrapper checks Docker Hub for a newer image at most once every 24 hours, and AI_MEMORY_NO_VERSION_CHECK=1 turns that off. Updates in an air gap are manual, the same way as the install. Read the offline install page.

capacity.title: Capacity
capacity.text: Every write goes through one writer. The project measured where that stops, with cargo test -p ai-memory-store --test writer_throughput -- --ignored --nocapture.
notes: The ceiling is about 700 writes per second, reached near 32 writers.
The write queue is bounded at 1024. Past that, producers slow down and every write still lands.
Shell hooks give up on the server after 200 ms and spool the event locally, so a slow server does not stall your agent.
AI_MEMORY_HOOK_RATE_PER_SEC and AI_MEMORY_HOOK_RATE_BURST add an optional rate limit per actor and session. It is off by default.

caveats.title: Read the numbers with their caveats
caveats.text: They were taken on a fast local disk, and the cost is fsync, so a network filesystem or a slow volume will be materially lower. They measure the store and not the HTTP front door. The one published hook latency figure, about 145 ms per native hook call on one macOS host, is that host’s measurement and not a benchmark.

capacity.link: Read the capacity section of the deploy guide

upgrading.title: Upgrading
notes: With the Docker wrapper, this verifies and replaces the wrapper, pulls the image and restages hook scripts. A server on another host is upgraded separately.
Schema and wiki migrations run on start. They are forward-only: an older binary refuses to open a migrated directory, so run ai-memory backup first if you might roll back.

from1x.title: Coming from 1.x
from1x.text: The first 2.0 start rewrites the wiki to Open Knowledge Format v0.2. Before touching anything it archives the whole data directory to ~/ai-memory-backup-okf-v0.2-<date>.tar.gz (/data/backups/ in a container) and verifies the archive. If the backup cannot be written or verified, the migration aborts and the server refuses to start, with your data untouched.

upgrading.link: Read the 2.0 migration guide, including how to go back

faq.a: Not on a single-user laptop bound to 127.0.0.1, and not over stdio. Add a TLS proxy when accounts exist, when the server is bound beyond loopback, when you open the web UI from another machine, or when it is reachable beyond the LAN. ai-memory does not terminate TLS itself.

faq.q: What do I need to back up?
faq.a: Run ai-memory backup, which is safe while the server runs. The tarball holds the wiki tree, a consistent SQLite snapshot and config.toml. The wiki is the source of truth. Pages, links and search can be rebuilt from it with ai-memory reindex, but sessions, handoffs, users and keys exist only in the database.

It supports OIDC device auth for lifecycle hooks and CLI commands against any standards-compliant issuer. The server does not validate OIDC tokens itself, so putting the server API behind your identity provider requires an OIDC-aware gateway in front of it.

faq.q: Can two servers share one data directory?
faq.a: No. Run one server per data directory. Since 2.0 the server takes an exclusive lock on .serve.lock and a second server refuses to start.
